title: Python Control Flow: Learn if, for, while and match
author: Glenn Junsay Pansensoy
excerpt: Learn Python control flow with runnable code: if/elif/else, for and while loops, break, continue, pass and match/case
body: Back to Home 24 lessons Pyodide ready Master the flow of your programs: conditional statements, loops, break/continue/pass, and the new match/case statement. 24 interactive lessons with runnable code — crafted by @PoeticGlenn. Browse All Lessons Start Learning Everything about Python control flow — from basic conditionals to advanced loop control. Learn how to make decisions, repeat actions, and manage program execution with if, for, while, break, continue, pass, else with loops, nested loops, and the powerful match/case pattern matching introduced in Python 3.10. Each concept is broken down step-by-step with interactive code examples from @PoeticGlenn. 📖 Introduction Without control flow, programs would be simple sequences of instructions — they couldn't adapt, repeat, or make decisions. Control flow is what gives your programs intelligence and flexibility. This curriculum, designed by @PoeticGlenn, covers every aspect of Python's control flow, from the foundational if statement to the modern match/case pattern matching, ensuring you can write dynamic, efficient, and readable code. Conditionals let your program choose different paths based on data, user input, or state. Loops automate repetitive tasks, process collections, and iterate until conditions are met. Break, continue, and pass give you fine-grained control over loop execution and program flow. "The essence of programming is making decisions and repeating tasks — control flow is how we express that." — @PoeticGlenn 🐍 🚀 Why Learn This Curriculum Every program that does anything interesting uses control flow. Whether it's a simple calculator or a complex AI system, the ability to make decisions and repeat actions is fundamental. This curriculum, curated by @PoeticGlenn, ensures you understand not only the syntax but the logic behind each control structure, empowering you to write programs that are both powerful and elegant. Master if/elif/else to handle complex conditions and make your programs smarter. for and while loops let you process data, repeat tasks, and build efficient algorithms. break, continue, and pass give you precision in loop management and placeholder logic. Python 3.10's match/case brings structural pattern matching, making code cleaner and more expressive. @PoeticGlenn says: "Control flow is the skeleton of your program. Get it right, and everything else falls into place." 🌍 Significance in the Programming World Every programming language has conditionals and loops. They are the building blocks of algorithms and the foundation of structured programming. Python's control flow is clean, intuitive, and powerful, making it an ideal language for learning and applying these concepts. This curriculum, designed by @PoeticGlenn, gives you transferable skills that apply to any language you learn in the future. Conditionals and loops exist in every language — learn them once, use them everywhere. Control flow is the backbone of algorithms — from sorting to searching to AI. Control flow structures define the shape and logic of your entire program. "Control flow is the art of deciding what happens next — and that's what programming is all about." Jump to any section — all entries are equal size 📖 Introduction 🚀 Why Learn This 🌍 Significance 🔀 if/elif/else 🔄 for Loop ⏳ while Loop ⏹️ break & continue 🚫 pass 🏁 else with Loops 🧩 Nested Loops 🎯 match/case ❓ FAQ 💛 Outro Make decisions in your code based on boolean conditions. The simplest conditional: execute a block only if the condition is True. Step 1: Define a condition, e.g., age = 18. Step 2: Write if age >= 18:. Step 3: Indent the block to execute when the condition is true. python Copy Run age = 18 if age >= 18: print("You are an adult.") print("You can vote.") Handle both True and False cases. Step 1: Check temperature > 30. Step 2: If true, print hot message; else, print not hot. python Copy Run temperature = 25 if temperature > 30: print("It's hot outside.") else: print("It's not too hot.") Chain multiple conditions with elif. Step 1: Assign score = 85. Step 2: Check conditions from top to bottom. Step 3: Execute the first true block. python Copy Run score = 85 if score >= 90: print("Grade: A") elif score >= 80: print("Grade: B") elif score >= 70: print("Grade: C") elif score >= 60: print("Grade: D") else: print("Grade: F") Iterate over sequences like lists, tuples, strings, and ranges. Iterate over items in a collection. Step 1: Create a list: colors = ["red", "green", "blue"]. Step 2: Use for color in colors:. Step 3: Print each color. python Copy Run colors = ["red", "green", "blue"] for color in colors: print(f"Color: {color}") range() generates a sequence of numbers for iteration. Step 1: Use range(5) to generate 0–4. Step 2: Use range(1, 6) for 1–5. Step 3: Use range(0, 10, 2) for even numbers. python Copy Run print("range(5):") for i in range(5): print(i, end=" ") print("\n") print("range(1, 6):") for i in range(1, 6): print(i, end=" ") print("\n") print("range(0, 10, 2):") for i in range(0, 10, 2): print(i, end=" ") Get both index and value while iterating. Step 1: Use enumerate() on a list. Step 2: Unpack index and value in the loop. python Copy Run fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"] for index, fruit in enumerate(fruits): print(f"{index}: {fruit}") Execute a block repeatedly while a condition is true. Use when you don't know the number of iterations in advance. Step 1: Initialize a counter count = 0. Step 2: Write while count < 5:. Step 3: Print count and increment. python Copy Run count = 0 while count < 5: print(f"Count: {count}") count += 1 print("Loop finished!") ⚠️ Ensure the condition eventually becomes False to avoid infinite loops. Keep asking until valid input is received. Step 1: Set valid = False. Step 2: While not valid, ask for input and validate. python Copy Run valid = False while not valid: response = input("Enter a positive number: ") try: num = float(response) if num > 0: valid = True print(f"Thank you! You entered {num}") else: print("Number must be positive.") except ValueError: print("That's not a valid number.") Fine-tune loop execution: exit early or skip iterations. Terminate the loop immediately. Step 1: Loop over numbers 1–10. Step 2: If number is 5, break. python Copy Run for i in range(1, 11): if i == 5: print("Breaking at 5") break print(i) Skip the rest of the current iteration and move to the next. Step 1: Loop over numbers 0–9. Step 2: If number is even, continue. Step 3: Print only odd numbers. python Copy Run for i in range(10): if i % 2 == 0: continue print(i) Do nothing — use as a placeholder where syntax requires a statement. pass is often used in function stubs, class stubs, and loops that need a placeholder. Step 1: Define a function that does nothing yet. Step 2: Use pass in a loop to skip processing. python Copy Run def future_function(): pass print("Defined a placeholder function") for i in range(3): if i == 1: pass print(i) 💡 pass is not a comment — it's a valid Python statement that does nothing. It's useful for scaffolding code. The else block runs if the loop completes without a break. Useful for search patterns: execute else if item not found. Step 1: Search for a target in a list. Step 2: If found, break. If not, the else runs. python Copy Run items = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] target = 3 for item in items: if item == target: print(f"Found {target}!") break else: print(f"{target} not found.") Use nested loops to iterate over multi-dimensional data or generate combinations. Iterate over rows and columns of a grid. Step 1: Outer loop over rows. Step 2: Inner loop over columns. Step 3: Print a multiplication table. python Copy Run for i in range(1, 4): for j in range(1, 4): print(f"{i}*{j}={i*j:2}", end=" ") print() Modern and powerful alternative to long if/elif chains for structural pattern matching. Match a value against multiple patterns. Step 1: Use match with a subject. Step 2: Define case patterns. Step 3: Use _ as wildcard. python Copy Run def describe_number(n): match n: case 0: return "zero" case 1: return "one" case 2: return "two" case _: return "other" print(describe_number(0)) print(describe_number(2)) print(describe_number(5)) Match data structures and add conditions with guards. Step 1: Match a tuple (x, y). Step 2: Use if guard for additional condition. python Copy Run def location(point): match point: case (0, 0): return "origin" case (0, y): return f"on y-axis at {y}" case (x, 0): return f"on x-axis at {x}" case (x, y) if x == y: return f"on diagonal line at ({x}, {y})" case _: return "somewhere else" print(location((0, 0))) print(location((0, 5))) print(location((3, 0))) print(location((3, 3))) print(location((1, 2))) Common questions about control flow in Python, answered. + break exits the loop entirely, while continue skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next one. + Use while when the number of iterations is unknown, such as when waiting for user input or processing data until a condition is met. Use for when iterating over a known sequence. + The else block runs if the loop completes without a break. It's useful for search patterns: "if not found, do something". + No, match/case was introduced in Python 3.10. For older versions, use if/elif chains or dictionaries for dispatching. + Yes, pass is commonly used as a placeholder in functions, classes, or loops that you haven't implemented yet. It prevents syntax errors. + You can use a flag variable, or wrap the loops in a function and use return. Python doesn't have a "break out of all loops" statement. + elif is short for "else if". It allows you to check multiple conditions sequentially. Only the first true condition's block executes. From conditionals to loops, from break to match/case, you now have a complete understanding of how to direct the flow of your Python programs. You can make decisions, repeat actions, and handle complex branching with confidence.
